Power system flexibility seen as key for integrating renewables into electricity grids
Experts say power system flexibility is crucial for integrating renewable energy sources like solar and wind into modern grids. Flexibility markets now pay participants for adjusting generation or consumption when needed by grid operators.
Power system flexibility is increasingly important for the secure and cost-effective integration of renewable energy sources, according to an Oct. 7 article citing the International Energy Agency. The agency said that increased flexibility allows the electricity system to "stretch" and "contract" without causing supply interruptions or failures.
The shift toward renewables such as solar and wind has changed how electricity is generated, creating operational challenges due to their variable and intermittent nature. Adolfo Núñez Sarompas, professor at the Faculty of Business and Technology at Universidad a Distancia de Madrid (UDIMA), said, “Electricity has to be generated and supplied reliably, continuously and at the required level of quality. The growth of renewables has changed the generation curve.” He added that because solar output varies throughout the day and wind conditions can change rapidly, generation needs to be much more flexible.
Núñez also said that increasing electrification in sectors like industry makes flexibility essential for integrating large amounts of renewables without compromising security of supply. By 2025, he noted that keeping power systems balanced will require flexible mechanisms supported by various technologies.
The Institute for Research in Technology professors stated, “Renewables are and will remain essential to decarbonizing the economy. They are also cost-competitive with other technologies, but their main drawback is the intermittency and uncertainty of their output. Only a flexible power system can integrate renewables while maintaining security of supply.”
Flexibility markets have emerged as mechanisms where participants are paid for their ability to adjust generation or consumption when needed by the grid. Participants include industrial consumers, renewable generators like solar or wind farms, households, and demand aggregators—intermediaries who combine flexible consumption from multiple users into a single resource offered on these markets. Andrés Ramos and José Pablo Chaves explained, “A demand aggregator (or flexibility aggregator) is an intermediary that combines the flexible consumption of multiple users so it can be managed as a single resource...and offers that flexibility to electricity markets or transmission or distribution system operators.”
Núñez recalled changes over time: “Twenty years ago...the electricity market was balanced by adjusting the output of a small number of power plants. Today there are tens of thousands of small and medium-sized generators and consumers that can use their own resources to provide the flexibility the system needs.” He also noted benefits from decentralized energy models which allow local management, reduce dependence on large plants, improve responses during disruptions such as floods or fires, reduce transmission losses, and may lower investment needs in new infrastructure.
